c: Chapter 74: The profile editor and profile building blocks
p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
x: A syntax profile tells Pilcrow what your markup means. This chapter describes the profile editor control by control, and then lists every building block a profile can use. For a task-based introduction, see Chapter 37 to Chapter 39. Open the editor from Settings ▸ Library ▸ Syntax Profiles: New starts a profile, Edit changes a custom one, and Duplicate copies a built-in profile so you can change the copy. The editor's title is Edit Profile, with Cancel, Save and Profile Help (which opens the in-app reference to these building blocks). On a narrow screen, a Profile section switch chooses between Overview, Rules and Test Sample; on a wide one all three show at once.

c: Chapter 74: The profile editor and profile building blocks
p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
x: Field What it does Name The profile's name, shown in the status bar menu and Settings. Description A note about the profile. File extensions (comma-separated) The extensions that choose this profile for a file. Two profiles cannot share an extension. Inherits None, or another profile whose rules this one builds on. Syntax Extends Markdown or Replaces Markdown (below). At a glance Counts of Block rules, Inline rules and Nesting rules. Edit Advanced JSON… Opens the profile as JSON for fields the guided editor does not expose. Apply keeps your JSON changes; Cancel discards them. Extends Markdown adds your rules to Markdown's: its headings, lists, emphasis and the rest are still read, and your block and inline rules add to them. A rule that is an unchanged copy of one of the CommonMark profile's describes what Markdown already does, and is left to it. Replaces Markdown makes your rules the whole syntax, so Markdown constructs stop being recognized. With it, one rule must produce End of line, or nothing separates into paragraphs. The editor warns "Add a rule whose output node is "newline", or nothing will separate into paragraphs", and the profile cannot be saved until one exists. It also lists any output types the profile does not define.

c: Chapter 74: The profile editor and profile building blocks
p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
x: Rules come in three groups. A block rule recognizes whole lines and blocks. Add rule adds one. Each rule has a Pattern, a Match type, what it Produces, and Options. A rule is removed with its Delete button. With none, the editor says "No rules yet. Add one to recognize a block construct." An inline rule recognizes text inside a line. Add inline rule adds one. Inline rules offer four match types (Literal prefix, Literal exact, Regex (bounded) and Delimiter pair); block rules offer all seven. Nesting rules say which outputs may sit inside which. Each has a Parent node and Allowed children (comma separated). Empty means unrestricted: "No restrictions. Every node type may nest inside any other." Add nesting rule adds one. Match type Reads the pattern as Block Inline Literal prefix Text the construct starts with. yes yes Literal exact The whole text of the construct. yes yes Line-start prefix Text at the start of a line, such as # . yes Indented block Lines that begin with the pattern, such as four spaces or a tab. Consecutive ones, and blank lines between them, are one block, shown without the indent. yes Fenced block A line that opens a block, closed by a matching line. yes Regex (bounded) A regular expression. Pilcrow warns before saving one that could get stuck: "This regex could hang the editor — simplify it." yes yes Delimiter pair The same mark on both sides of text on one line, such as %% in %%this%%. There is no space just inside the marks. yes yes In a regular expression, (?<name>…) names a part of the match. See Named parts below.

c: Chapter 74: The profile editor and profile building blocks
p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
x: Each rule's Options group offers: Option What it does Priority Rules with a higher priority are tried first. Only at the start of a line Keeps a rule from matching mid-line. Named parts become attributes Each named part of a regular expression becomes an attribute of the output. The editor lists "Parts in this pattern" and "Parts this output reads". For an output that holds text, such as bold or a link, the text shown is the part named text if there is one, else the last part that matched. Produces What the rule makes: an output from the lists below, or a Custom name. Custom node name The name for a Custom output. Fixed attributes Parts that have the same value every time, added with Add attribute (a Name and a Value). A value may include a named part, written {name}: an e-mail rule whose pattern names the address can give its link the url mailto:{address}. Insert text What the Insert menu writes for this rule, exactly as it should appear, with $0 where the caret should go. A rule matched by a regular expression, a block or indentation needs this, or the Insert menu leaves it out. Only after a blank line For an indented block: an indented line right after text stays part of that text, such as a list item's next line. After Return at the end of a line For lists and quotes: Automatic (repeats bullets and quotes, counts up numbered items, and starts task items unchecked), Repeat the marker, Count up, Start fresh from the marker, or Add nothing. For a Fenced block rule, Block holds says what is inside: Choice Meaning Nothing yet Not set. Text, shown as written Code or preformatted text. Nothing — hidden A comment, left out of the document. Other blocks, in a box A quote, sidebar or admonition holding paragraphs, lists and more. Other blocks, no box The blocks join the surrounding text; the lines only group them. A table See Tables, below. A table drawn in text A grid or aligned columns of text that runs from its opening line to the next blank line, such as reStructuredText's. Indented text under a line ending in a marker The opening line is prose that ends in the marker, as reStructuredText's :: does; the prose stays a paragraph, and the text set in under it after a blank line is shown as written. Indented text under an opening line A directive such as .. code-block::, which holds the indented lines under it and has no closing line. Closing line is the line that ends the block; empty means the same line as the opening one ("Same as the opening line"). A delimiter that is not a regular expression, such as +++, is matched as plain text. Closing line repeats the opening mark, at least as often is for Markdown-style fences: the closing line is the opening line's first character repeated at least as many times, so a longer fence holds a shorter one as text. A text block's language, when the opening line names a known one, is coloured in the editor. A table block's options: Option What it does Layout Grid with rule lines (cells between | with a rule line between rows) or Aligned columns (columns lined up under a first rule line). Cell separator The text that starts each cell. Rule line pattern, Header rule line pattern Lines that draw only a rule, and the one that ends the header. Row ends with A mark that ends each row, as a LaTeX tabular does. Spanning cell pattern A cell that spans columns. Cell options pattern A regular expression for what may come just before a cell's separator; a part named colspan makes the cell span that many columns. Column list separator, Repeat marker How a columns list is written: with , and *, 3* counts three columns. First line before a blank line is the header The header row is implied by layout. Formats Other ways to write the cells, each a name and a separator (such as csv and ,), added with Add format and chosen with the table's format part.

c: Chapter 74: The profile editor and profile building blocks
p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
x: Setting What it does Nest lists by marker Each new marker, such as ** after *, starts a deeper level, whatever the indentation. List continuation line A line, alone after a list item, that attaches the next block to the item. Keep single line breaks A line break inside a paragraph stays a line break. Give headings ids A heading with no id of its own gets one from its title: lower case, words joined by the word separator, after the prefix (Heading id prefix, Heading id word separator). With _ and _, "Getting Started" is _getting_started, so a cross-reference to it shows the title. A repeated title adds the separator and a number. Number headings Once the document defines the attribute named in When the document defines, such as AsciiDoc's :sectnums:, headings from From heading level down are numbered: 1., 1.1., 2.. Headings before the definition are not. Numbered captions A titled block of an output listed here, such as image, table or example, gets the Label and its own number before its title (for example "Figure 1."), at the Caption place, Above or Below the block. Added with Add caption.

c: Chapter 74: The profile editor and profile building blocks
p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
s: Inline marks that pair by what stands around them
x: A language such as Markdown writes bold and italic with a run of characters that opens or closes depending on the characters beside it, and a code span or link with brackets, so one pattern for the whole construct cannot find them. Turn on Read marks by what stands around them to describe them. Setting What it does Escape character A character that makes the next one plain. Code span character A run of this character opens a span that the next run of the same length closes. Run marks Marks that pair as runs, added with Add run mark. Each has a Mark, what One mark draws and what Two marks draw, and May open or close inside a word (off for _). Pair marks Marks that pair with a run of the same length, added with Add pair mark: the Mark, what it Draws, and Only when this setting is on, a syntax setting such as highlight that must be on (or Always). Links and web addresses Image prefix, Address written on its own is enclosed by, Schemes that begin a bare address, Line that defines a label has, and Footnote label begins with (the character after a label's opening bracket that makes it a footnote: [^note] is drawn as a footnote reference when a line begins [^note]:). Marks pair within a line. Code, escaped characters and a link's address are plain text to the marks around them.

c: Chapter 74: The profile editor and profile building blocks
p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
x: With Styled Source on, the editor draws a document in the look of its syntax: larger headings, bold and italic runs, quote bars, list indents, task boxes, rules, links and code cards, and hides the marks that make them (with Hide Markers on) except on the line the caret is on. The editor knows nothing about any one syntax: a rule says what its match is by carrying a styling entry, and a rule without one is coloured but not restyled. Every rule's Options has a Styled source group: Field What it does Role What the match is, or Not styled. For one construct inside a line: heading, strong, emphasis, code, strike, highlight, underline, link, subscript, superscript. For a whole line: rule (a thematic break), list (a list item's marker, including its indent and the space after it), task (a marker followed by a checkbox) and quote (the > marks of a quoted line). For a block recognized whole: codeBlock. For a block whose opening and closing lines are separate matches: quoteRegion. For a table, equation or diagram drawn as a picture: renderedBlock. Content group The capture group, counting from 1, that holds what the construct is about: the word inside *bold*, the title in \section{Title}. What the match has besides it is the construct's own marks, which Hide Markers hides. 0 means the whole match is content and nothing hides, as for a web address. Leave it out when the match is only marks, such as a heading's == . Heading level, Level group A heading's level, 1 to 6. Left out, it is the number at the end of the rule's output name (heading2), or the length of the capture group that holds a run of #. Marker group For a list or task, the capture group that is the marker with its indent and the spaces after it, when the match begins with something else, such as the > of a quoted item. Styles to the end of the line Styles from the match to the end of the line, for a rule that matches only a heading's marker and leaves its title as the text that follows. Draws as For a rendered block, what it is: a table, math or diagram, or Not a picture. Address groups For a link, the capture groups, tried in order, that hold the address it opens when clicked or tapped; 0 is the whole match. Only web, mail and telephone addresses open. The group numbers count the pattern's parentheses from 1; 0 is the whole match. A profile that does not replace Markdown also keeps Markdown's own reading of the kinds its rules do not declare, such as its quote bars and the pairs of **.

c: Chapter 74: The profile editor and profile building blocks
p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
x: A Document attribute rule defines a value by name, and an Attribute reference rule (an inline rule with parts name and original) replaces a reference with it. A reference to an attribute no one has defined stays as written. A Conditional section keeps or drops the blocks between its lines, depending on whether the attributes it names are set. Attributes apply from where they are defined onwards. A rule producing Settings for the next block recognizes a whole line that configures the block after it and shows nothing itself. Its parts and fixed attributes are given to that block: title, id, nodeType, language and hardbreaks have the meanings listed under Parts, and any other part is kept on the block, where a table, list or quote reads it.

c: Chapter 74: The profile editor and profile building blocks
p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
x: Parts are the named pieces of a match that an output reads. Part Meaning allOf The separator between names when all of them are needed, such as +. alt An image's description, for readers who cannot see it. anyOf The separator between names when any one of them is enough, such as ,. attribution Who said a quote, shown under it. citetitle The work a quote comes from, shown after the attribution. columns A table's column list, such as 1,2,1; its entries count the columns. condition The attribute names the section depends on. conditionType defined keeps the section when the attributes are set, undefined when they are not. content The text itself, when it is not the whole match. format A diagram's engine (mermaid or vega-lite); for a table, which of its delimited formats the cells use. hardbreaks When present, keeps the next block's single line breaks. header Any value but false makes a table's first row its header. id A name: for the next block, the id cross-references point to; for a footnote, a name that lets later footnotes with no text of their own share its number. keys The keys to press, separated by commas. label The text shown for a reference or anchor, in place of the target's own title. language A code block's programming language, used for its coloring. level The heading level, from 1 to 6. marker The separator after the term, such as ::. A different marker nests a list inside the description. name The attribute's name, in a definition or a reference. nodeType Makes the next block into another output, by its name in the file. noHeader When present, a table has no header row. notation The maths notation: tex (the default) or latex. open true shows a collapsible section open. ordered true makes the list numbered. original The reference as written, shown when the attribute is not defined. presentation How the next description list is shown: sideBySide puts terms and descriptions in two columns; questions numbers each term as a question, with its answer under it. primary The index entry. secondary A sub-entry under the index entry. sectionLabel A word the next heading's number follows, such as Appendix: such headings are counted on their own, Appendix A:. sectionLabelStart The first of those numbers: a letter (A) counts in letters, a number in numbers. src The address of the video or audio file. start The number a numbered list starts at. summary The line shown on a collapsible section while it is closed. targetID The id the reference points to. term The term being described. tertiary A sub-entry under the secondary one. text The text shown, when the pattern captures more than that. A footnote's text follows the paragraph, table or list it is in, numbered. title A title: a box's heading, an image's or link's tooltip, or a caption above the next block. type The kind of admonition, such as note, tip or warning. unset When present, the rule removes the attribute instead of defining it. url The address a link or image points to. value The attribute's value; references to attributes defined earlier are replaced in it.

p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
x: Edit Render Theme styles Preview, HTML, PDF, image and print output. Its Pilcrow custom properties also set Word styles. A Render Theme does not style the app or the editor. Part What it does Name The theme's name. Appearance Automatic, Light or Dark. CSS The stylesheet, in a code editor. See Chapter 80 for the properties and classes. Rendered preview A specimen document drawn with your CSS as you type, so you can see the effect. CSS diagnostics Problems Pilcrow found in the CSS, such as a remote resource that is not allowed. Cancel, Save Close or keep the theme. Closing with changes asks Discard theme changes? with Discard Changes or Keep Editing. Baseline Reset to Baseline discards every change since the theme was created, duplicated or imported (after you confirm). Set as New Baseline saves the theme and makes its current state the restore point.

c: Chapter 75: The theme editors
p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
x: Edit Application Theme styles Pilcrow itself: its appearance, accent, sidebar, bars and editor. Part What it does Name The theme's name. Appearance Automatic, Light or Dark. An Automatic theme has two palettes. Editing colours for For an Automatic theme, Light or Dark: which of its two palettes you are editing. Colours, in five groups App (the accent), Sidebar (background and foreground), Status and formatting bars (background and foreground), Editor (background, foreground, cursor, selection, gutter background, gutter foreground, current-line rule), and Syntax (heading, marker, code, link, muted, and code keyword, string, number and comment). Each colour shows Default until you set one, and a Reset button puts it back. Preview A miniature of Pilcrow, with a sidebar, an editor and a status bar, in the colours you chose, in light or dark. c: Chapter 76: The macro editor
p: Part XIX · Editors for library items
x: Open the macro editor from Settings ▸ Library ▸ Macros: New inside a collection, or Edit on a macro. Its title is New Macro or Edit Macro. Field What it does Name A label for the macro. Trigger (for example /sig) The text that starts it. A macro expands when you type the trigger followed by a space, tab or return. Match How the trigger is read: Exact text, Prefix, or Regular expression. A regular expression that could hang the editor is refused: "That regular expression could hang the editor. Simplify it." Replacement The text it expands to. Insert Date/Time A menu that adds a date or time token to the replacement. Enabled Turns the macro on or off without deleting it. c: Chapter 80: The Render Theme CSS reference
p: Part XXI · File formats and limits
x: A Render Theme is CSS. It styles Preview, HTML, PDF, image and print output, and the Word styles listed at the end of this chapter. A Render Theme may be a single .css file or part of a ZIP package with local assets. Syntax profiles define how source text becomes the document; Render Themes only style the result. c: Chapter 80: The Render Theme CSS reference
p: Part XXI · File formats and limits
x: Pilcrow applies styles in this order: Pilcrow's structural reset; the selected theme CSS; one-off CSS from the export panel (Advanced options ▸ Custom CSS); required print and rendering corrections. c: Chapter 80: The Render Theme CSS reference
p: Part XXI · File formats and limits
x: Pilcrow reads theme CSS with a standard CSS tokenizer, so escapes are decoded before anything is checked: u\72 l(…) is a url() and @im\70 ort is an @import. Every place a browser would load from is checked: url(…), url("…"), src("…"), and strings inside image-set(). Each must be one of: a package-relative path (fonts/Body.woff2, ./paper.png). A ?query or #fragment is allowed and ignored when the file is looked up; a data: URL of type PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG (image/svg+xml), TTF, OTF, WOFF or WOFF2; a fragment reference such as url(#shadow), which names an element in the page. Anything with a scheme other than data: (https:, file:, blob:) or starting with // is refused, as is a path that starts with / or contains ...

c: Chapter 80: The Render Theme CSS reference
p: Part XXI · File formats and limits
x: A ZIP package can hold Render Themes (.css) and Application Themes (.json) together; each is listed with its own kind in Settings. A ZIP with at most one CSS file and at most one Application Theme needs no manifest. Anything more needs pilcrow-theme.json, which lists every theme under variants[].file. The file's extension decides its kind: { "id": "com.example.paper", "name": "Paper", "version": "1.0.0", "author": "Example Author", "license": "MIT", "cssAPIVersion": 1, "variants": [ { "id": "app", "name": "Paper", "file": "Paper.json", "appearance": "automatic" }, { "id": "light", "name": "Paper Light", "file": "Paper-Light.css", "appearance": "light" }, { "id": "dark", "name": "Paper Dark", "file": "Paper-Dark.css", "appearance": "dark" } ] } The manifest describes the package and its themes. It never contains style values: those are in the CSS and Application Theme files. The package id names the install folder. It must not start with . or have leading or trailing spaces. Installing a package whose id is already installed replaces it. A ZIP made with Finder's Compress works as is. Pilcrow skips __MACOSX/, ._*, .DS_Store and Thumbs.db, and when every file sits inside one top-level folder, that folder is treated as the package root. Deleting one theme removes it from the package and keeps the others along with the shared assets. Deleting the last theme removes the package. A deleted theme that was selected returns that selection to its kind's default: Automatic for the Application Theme, Light for the Render Theme. CSS may reference packaged PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, TTF, OTF, WOFF and WOFF2 files with relative url(...) paths. Pilcrow verifies their signatures and embeds referenced assets as data URLs so rendering and exported HTML remain offline and self-contained. ZIP paths cannot escape the package, collide by case, or point to links. Archive size, entry count, individual size and compression ratio are bounded.
